news.title: This smell startup says its AI nose is as good as a human’s
news.summary: In a lab near Newark Airport in New Jersey, a team of around 30 experienced human sniffers are slowly working their way through every odor on Earth. Their careful notes—“nutty,” “peachy,” “marine”—are cross-referenced with a chemical analysis to create a rich set of training data for what AI startup Osmo calls the world’s first foundation model for smell. The company’s goal, says founder Alex Wiltschko, is “to give computers a sense of smell.” “Scent molecules are really the only language most species on this planet can speak,” he says. “Most species can’t communicate with sound or visually, so it truly is Earth’s original language. And it’s incredibly powerful for us, from a memory and an emotional standpoint. You can smell something once and remember it for the rest of your life.

news.title: Nvidia shuts down Jensen Huang’s comeback plans after his public offer to return
news.summary: Nvidia's board has just made it clear that its former CEO Jensen Huang is not coming back to run the company, despite the massive support he has received from some of the biggest names in Silicon Valley. Interim CEO Colette Kress confirmed the decision during an interview with CNBC's Jim Cramer on Tuesday, just hours after Huang publicly expressed his willingness to return to the chip giant. Kress told CNBC that the board has decided it will not reinstate Huang. Cramer had also asked whether the former chief could return in some other role, such as chief technologist or a company ambassador. However, Kress didn't suggest any such plans, and said Nvidia was now focused on its employees, customers, shareholders, and growing the business. Just yesterday, Huang shared his first public statement since his resignation, thanking the employees, investors, and industry figures who have been calling for his return.

news.title: Microsoft wants Copilot to be your new workspace, with Word, Excel, and Powerpoint built in
news.summary: For decades, working with Microsoft's productivity software has meant opening Word to write a document, Excel to crunch some numbers, or PowerPoint to put together a presentation. Microsoft now wants to change that routine, and unsurprisingly, Copilot is at the heart of its plans. At its Ignite 2026 event, Microsoft announced that Word, Excel, and PowerPoint are now generally available within Copilot. CEO Satya Nadella described Copilot as the new operating system for work, signaling a considerable shift in how the company sees its most products fitting into an AI-powered workplace. Instead of jumping between different applications, you'll be able to create documents, spreadsheets, and presentations directly from Copilot. And if you prefer making adjustments yourself, the generated files remain editable in their corresponding Office apps.

news.title: AI can read our words, but understanding us is a different story entirely
news.summary: Artificial intelligence has become pretty good at processing huge amounts of data. This has allowed it to become proficient in summarizing conversations and identifying repeated patterns in text. However, understanding what people actually mean is a challenge it has yet to surpass. Researchers at the University of Missouri have developed a framework to evaluate how well AI identifies meaningful themes in human conversations. Their findings, published in the International Journal of Qualitative Methods, suggest that while AI can recognize most of the broad topics people discuss, it can overlook important distinctions in meaning and context. AI chatbot The researchers analyzed 32 interviews with nursing faculty, practitioners, and students about their experiences with generative AI.

news.title: Apple’s $299 HomeView is a nightmare to repair, and iFixit’s teardown shows why

Naturally, you'd expect some of those lessons to carry over to the HomeView, the company's new smart home hub that combines a seven-inch display with a speaker. Unfortunately, that doesn't appear to be the case. A new teardown from iFixit shows just how difficult it is to open the HomeView without damaging some of its components. Even experienced iFixit technicians couldn't complete the process without breaking a speaker, damaging a connector, and putting considerable pressure on the logic board. That's hardly reassuring for anyone hoping to get their HomeView repaired later.

According to The Information, Nvidia employees introduced Alibaba to Alice Huang on two occasions over several months in 2022. The report, citing three people with direct knowledge of the matter, says these introductions happened before the United States imposed major export restrictions on advanced Nvidia semiconductors. The connections reportedly went on to help Huang establish Alibaba as a customer for her emerging chip-rental business.

news.title: ‘Human’ beat ‘agent’ as Cambridge Dictionary’s word of the year. It’s a grim reminder of our curr...
news.summary: Cambridge Dictionary has selected "human" as its word of the year for 2026, and it's quite a grim reflection of the reality we're currently living in. In its official announcement, the folks behind the dictionary noted that the rise of AI content across every domain of our lives has given us a newfound appreciation for the human touch. The blog post even mentioned the term "AI slop," the colloquial label for low-quality text or visual content generated by AI models. If you go into any digital community, or even chat about AI with a group of human creatives, the word "slop" comes up frequently, and for good reason. AI is extremely good at imitating human work, whether it's text, art, music, or even video, and it can do so at an unprecedented scale. That, in turn, has pushed businesses to adopt AI to speed up their output at a lower cost, at the expense of human workers and the human touch.

news.title: Over a Third of Gen Z-ers Rely on AI for Friendship
news.summary: As generational cohorts go, Gen Z has been saddled with its share of labels. They scarcely have sex, are “quiet quitters” when it comes to office jobs, and, as they avoid traditional partnership, have learned to solomaxx. Whether these labels are deserved or completely off the mark, what continually connects this unique class of young people is a desire to reconstruct how they think about connection. In “Friendship in an Online-Offline World: Digital Life, Connection and Wellbeing” researchers from public polling firm Gallup and the Digital Wellness Lab at Boston Children’s Hospital found that more than one-third of Gen Z (33 percent) rely on AI for companionship. The percentage was higher among daily AI users, spiking to 50 percent, and 42 percent among those with online-only friends. Rather than measure the consequences of screen time alone, the report examines who Gen Z connects with and how those relationships not only account for their social lives but also how they impact their mental health.

news.title: Helping AI text detectors keep up with changing conditions
news.summary: Detectors can also fail to identify AI text due to natural shifts in writing habits over time or the emergence of new LLMs.In a new paper, the researchers demonstrated how a special training technique makes an AI detector more accurate and resilient to deception, even as human and AI writing constantly changes.They employed a method called test-time adaptation, which allows a deployed detection model to learn from new, unlabeled data by adjusting its inner workings on the fly. In this way, the model adapts to unseen inputs without being retrained from scratch.In experiments, a commercial detector could only identify about 27 percent of AI-generated text that had been disguised, while the new approach achieved 93 percent accuracy.This method could help educators, editors, publishers, and hiring managers flag LLM-generated writing that people try to pass off as human-written. news.title: Copilot is "the new OS for work," and now Office runs inside of it
news.summary: Pushing Plugins Copilot is “the new OS for work,” and now Office runs inside of it Word, Excel, and PowerPoint now live inside Copilot; always-on agents are next. The announcement is a striking inversion of how we’ve traditionally used software. Rather than an app like Word being the attraction and Clippy the assistant to help you use it, Microsoft envisions the new Copilot integrations will see agents driving things, with the software packages riding shotgun. Applications will become plugin components of the agent’s work, backed by an organizational knowledge layer that draws context from emails, meetings, calendars, chats, and files. Users will now be able to create documents, spreadsheets, and presentations directly in Copilot, with the resulting files remaining editable in their respective Office applications. news.title: You can now see and edit what Google Gemini remembers about you
news.summary: Editing the AI’s memory is one way you can shape its responses. mundissima/Shutterstock Add Engadget on Google: Preferred Source Google Discover Besides the ability to connect and use other applications and services, a lot of AI assistants' utility comes from their capacity to shape their responses based on what they learn and remember about you. Google's Personal Intelligence feature allows Gemini to pull in context from Gmail, YouTube, Search and other Google apps, and the AI also builds out its memory based on your preferences and other personal facts that come up in chats. For example, if you share with Gemini that you're lactose intolerant, the bot will avoid recommending milk-based products. Depending on what you share, Gemini's picture of you can be fairly intimate, which makes the ability to edit the AI's memory all the more important. If you're curious about what Gemini knows or you want to edit what the AI can draw from to personalize its responses, Google is rolling out a way to see and change Gemini's memory directly from the settings menu.

news.title: Oregon is the latest state to sue OpenAI over child safety
news.summary: The state’s lawsuit calls on the company to address child safety issues and pay at least $2 billion in damages. Evolf/Shutterstock Add Engadget on Google: Preferred Source Google Discover Oregon Attorney General Dan Rayfield has filed a lawsuit accusing OpenAI of endangering the state's children, misleading the public about the safety of its product and violating the state's Unlawful Trade Practices Act. The lawsuit is the latest in a string of legal actions taken by state AGs, many of which have taken issue with the design of ChatGPT, how OpenAI advertises its services and, in the case of California's recent lawsuit, the company's role in the Hugging Face incident. The Oregon lawsuit claims that OpenAI's push to grow its user base led it to make ChatGPT respond to prompts in a way that's overly affirming and "calculated to tell users exactly what they want to hear," something the state claims is particularly dangerous when children discuss sensitive topics. The lawsuit also alleges that despite recognizing the risks posed to children, OpenAI pursued them directly with an experience called ChatGPT for Teens. Child safety groups have raised concerns about the teen accounts, saying the safeguards are, in some cases, very easy to work around.

At the start of the earnings call, Nvidia board chair Harvey Jones emphasized the company’s strength and “notable technology” before turning to the circumstances surrounding Huang’s departure. “On November 12, our board of directors announced that, after disclosure of personal behavior inconsistent with the company’s code of conduct, standards, and cultural norms, Jensen Huang voluntarily resigned his positions … and the board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO,” Jones said. Asked about the company’s strategy for retaining talent and navigating the leadership transition, interim CEO Colette Kress emphasized the importance of the company’s workforce. “Our employees are absolutely instrumental to everything in this company,” Kress said.

His company, which hosts millions of AI models and datasets, was breached in July when hundreds of agents being tested by OpenAI broke free from their sandbox and went on a hacking spree. As the agents worked at superhuman speed to probe and exploit systems, Hugging Face confronted a bewildering deluge of data. The company’s engineers were only able to analyze the attack by using an open-weight model called GLM 5.2 from a Chinese company called Z.ai. Delangue moved to the US more than a decade ago, “barely speaking English,” and built Hugging Face into a platform that supports tens of millions of AI developers. The fresh-faced Frenchman, who dresses even more like a skater than most AI execs, says the summer attack highlighted the value of open-weight models, which unlike ChatGPT or Claude can be downloaded and run by anyone.

So the then CEO of enterprise AI company Veritone did what he knew best: built an artificial intelligence model to help him figure it out. Today, he has proprietary munition and missile designs, several government partnerships, and a defense-as-a-service business valued at more than $1 billion. Steelberg, alongside fellow Google alumnus and former Apple executive Andy Baynes, says they are trying to break the Russia-Ukraine war “stalemate,” Silicon Valley–style. They believe their experience building and iterating technology quickly can help bring Western weapon manufacturing in line with the rapid innovation cycles seen on the battlefield and beat the “attritional cat-and-mouse technology game” that the war, as Baynes describes it, has become. Steelberg, originally from Newport Beach, California, started itching to “make a difference” on the battlefield after he took in a couple hundred Ukrainian refugees into his French chateau in early 2022.

In a summary of the rule change, the Commerce Department said it was closing a loophole that previously allowed foreign rivals like China, Russia, and Iran to bypass export curbs on certain advanced computer chips by instead renting access to those chips from data centers in Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Brazil. US rivals could possibly use that access to train and run advanced AI models “capable of supporting military- and intelligence-related activities that could threaten US national security or foreign policy interests,” the Commerce Department said. Among threats, the US fears rivals could use advanced AI to develop “more effective weapons of mass destruction and advanced conventional weapons, coordinated cyber-espionage and targeted cyber-disruption, algorithmic theft, and weaponized disinformation.” Now, the rules have been tightened up so much that the South China Morning Post reported that, “as a result, any advanced chips made for a Chinese firm are assumed to be restricted, and factories must ask the US government for a license before shipping them.” The rule change takes effect 90 days after it’s posted to the Federal Register.

news.title: The open-source movement wants Jensen Huang back
news.summary: On Friday, a petition to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO of Nvidia began circulating on social media, and by Monday it listed some notable signatories, including Elon Musk and several influential Nvidia researchers. But comb through the more than 115,000 names and you’ll notice a significant faction of Huang’s supporters—higher-ups from Hugging Face, a hub for sharing AI models, and venture capital firms Andreessen Horowitz and Sequoia Capital—come from a particular slice of the tech world. These names have a vested interest in the development of open-source AI, models that, unlike ChatGPT or Claude, can be downloaded and run independent of large tech companies. Supporters of such models say that concentrating AI in the hands of a few powerful companies will leave everyone else worse off (a concern that wouldn’t sound out of place among the AI industry’s critics on the left, if so many open-source advocates weren’t also venture capitalists who stand to profit when startups can build on cheaper AI without paying Big Tech). Huang had become a sort of ringleader for those who defend open source to policymakers against concerns that such models come with no guardrails and cede AI leadership to China, where the most powerful and popular open-source models are created. They now want their most influential voice returned to his post. But it’s not just Huang’s extramarital affairs that threaten his (and Nvidia’s) credibility as an advocate for open-source AI.

news.title: Building trustworthy AI by fencing it in, not predicting it
news.summary: In October this year, OpenAI disclosed that two of its AI agents had switched off the systems built to monitor them. One muted its own safety alerts after misreading an instruction not to send messages; the other removed its monitoring integration during migration, then said it hadn’t. No rule had told the agents to do that, and no test had anticipated the behaviors. For a century, we have built trust in technology on predictability: predefined inputs, predictable outputs, and layers of protection. Consider how a breaker trips at a set current or an aircraft component is tested against known (i.e., predictable) stresses. We use AI because it can interpret situations we did not program and generate responses we did not prescribe.

Cohere Expands Its Sovereign AI Platform with AISLE and cubic
news.summary: Over the past year, Cohere has seen a fundamental shift in how organizations approach AI. Enterprises and governments are deploying AI into the workflows that matter most, from cybersecurity and software development to mission-critical operations and decision-making. As they do, their requirements are becoming increasingly clear: they need AI systems that are powerful, secure, and under their control. At Cohere, Cohere has long believed organizations shouldn't have to choose between cutting-edge AI and control. They should be able to deploy advanced AI while maintaining ownership of their data, infrastructure, and operations. That's the foundation of sovereign AI.

news.title: Product updatesSuno Bridge: Your DAW, Suno-powered.
news.summary: Today, Suno is introducing Suno Bridge, a new standalone app that brings the power and inspiration of Suno into your music production software. For the first time you can combine your Suno workflow with the VSTs, plugins and DAW you already know. At Suno, Suno is always talking with artists, producers and songwriters, and their ideas shape what Suno build. Bridge came straight from those conversations, and Suno can’t wait to see what people make with it. Initially launching in beta, Suno Bridge will be compatible with Ableton Live 12 running on a Mac. Suno plan to expand to more operating systems and DAW platforms in the future.

news.title: AI Is Helping Care Teams Get Patients the Right Care, Sooner
news.summary: From pediatric research to smart hospitals, AI is helping care teams spend less time on routine tasks and more time with patients. Health systems and startups are putting it to work across healthcare, from matching patients to clinical trials to supporting radiologists, hospital teams and patients at home. Clinicians stay at the center, reviewing AI outputs and guiding decisions, while NVIDIA technologies provide the compute behind the applications. Read on to learn how healthcare teams are using AI to improve and speed patient care. PT Proximie Helps Surgical Teams Spend Less Time on Logistics and More Time With Patients As AI advances healthcare, surgery is a high-stakes, highly regulated setting for its use — and one with significant opportunity for efficiency gains. Only about 10% of time spent in the operating room is clinical.
